e.etymology: A spelling of Ellie, the pet form of Eleanor, Ellen, Elizabeth and other names beginning with El-. In Dutch and the Scandinavian languages Elly is a long-standing short form of Elisabeth.
namesakes: Elly May Clampett (daughter on The Beverly Hillbillies)
Elly De La Cruz (Cincinnati Reds shortstop)

e.etymology: From the place name, best known from New Zealand, which Dutch mapmakers named after the province of Zeeland, 'sea land'. As a given name it is recent, with Zeal and Zee as short forms.

assoc.t: New Zealand; also Zealand, Denmark's largest island

e.etymology: A feminine spelling of Corey, an English surname of uncertain origin, and a short form of Corinne and Cora, which come from Greek kore, 'maiden'.
namesakes: Coco Gauff (tennis champion, born Cori Gauff)

e.etymology: A modern American name of unclear origin, used alongside Kalia, Kaliyah and Khaliyah. The Kh- spelling echoes Arabic names such as Khalil and Khalida.
The Russian and Romanian form of Irene, from Greek eirene, 'peace', the name of the Greek goddess of peace and of several early saints.
A spelling of Jonathan shaped by John. Jonathan is Hebrew Yehonatan, 'God has given'; in the Bible he is the son of King Saul and the loyal friend of David.

e.meaning: from the dukedom of Clarence, named for Clare in Suffolk
e.etymology: From the title Duke of Clarence, named for the town of Clare in Suffolk and given to sons of English kings. It became a first name in the 19th century, helped by Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence.
namesakes: Clarence Darrow (defense lawyer in the Scopes trial)

assoc.t: Clarence, the guardian angel in It's a Wonderful Life

e.etymology: From the country, Old English Irland: the Old Irish name Eriu, a goddess who personified the island, plus land. Alec Baldwin and Kim Basinger named their daughter Ireland in 1995.
namesakes: Ireland Baldwin (model, daughter of Alec Baldwin and Kim Basinger)

assoc.t: Ireland, the island nation in the North Atlantic

e.etymology: A girls' name popular with Pakistani families. Baby-name sources gloss it as 'heavenly flower', but no clear Arabic or Urdu root is documented.
A modern respelling of Adeline in the Adalyn family, with the doubled d of Addison. Adeline is a French pet form of Adele, from Germanic adal, 'noble'.
Coined by George R. R. Martin for Daenerys Targaryen, the dragon queen of his A Song of Ice and Fire novels. The HBO series Game of Thrones made it a baby name in the 2010s.

assoc.t: Daenerys Targaryen, dragon queen of Game of Thrones

e.note: Belongs to one character, who ends the series by burning a city; expect Game of Thrones comments.

e.etymology: A respelling of Aidan, from Irish Aodhan, a pet form of Aodh, 'fire'. Aydan is also a separate Turkish girls' name meaning 'from the moon'.
From Denali, the Alaskan peak that is the highest in North America. The name is Koyukon Athabaskan and means 'the high one' or 'the tall one'.

assoc.t: Denali in Alaska, North America's highest mountain
GMC Denali, luxury trim of GMC trucks and SUVs

e.etymology: A modern coinage in the pattern of Kayla and Layla, built on Ray or Rae. Rayla is the Moonshadow elf heroine of the Netflix animated series The Dragon Prince.

assoc.t: Rayla, elf heroine of Netflix's The Dragon Prince

e.etymology: An American coinage of the 2000s from the rhyming family of Aiden, Jayden, Brayden and Kayden, here with an initial T.
A modern American blend of Jesse with the -iah ending of Josiah and Isaiah. The King James Bible has a similar name, Jesiah.
A Turkish name meaning 'very rare', from Arabic andar. Americans know it from Ender Wiggin, the child commander of Orson Scott Card's novel Ender's Game, where it is his nickname for Andrew.

assoc.t: Ender Wiggin, hero of the novel Ender's Game
the Ender Dragon and Endermen of Minecraft

e.etymology: From Sanskrit Shiva, the Hindu god, plus amsha, 'portion, share': 'a part of Shiva'. It is one of several fashionable Indian names ending in -ansh.
A pet form of Judith, Hebrew Yehudit, 'woman of Judea'. It became a given name in its own right and peaked in the 1940s, the era of Judy Garland.
namesakes: Judy Garland (Dorothy in The Wizard of Oz)
Judy Blume (author of Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret)

assoc.t: Judge Judy, TV courtroom judge
Judy Hopps, rabbit police officer in Zootopia
Judy of the Punch and Judy puppet shows

e.etymology: Spanish and Portuguese form of Letitia, from Latin laetitia, 'joy, gladness'. An obscure Saint Laetitia is venerated mainly in Spain.

e.meaning: from Jessenia, a South American palm
e.etymology: From Jessenia, the botanical name of a South American palm. The Mexican writer Yolanda Vargas Dulche made it a girls' name with the heroine of her story Yesenia, a hit 1970 telenovela.
From the Latin name Maurus, 'Moor', a man from Mauretania in North Africa, and so 'dark-skinned'. Saint Maurus was a 6th-century follower of Saint Benedict.
From an English surname that began as a Norman French nickname, ourson, 'bear cub', from Latin ursus, 'bear'. In the medieval romance Valentine and Orson, Orson is raised by a bear.
namesakes: Orson Welles (director and star of Citizen Kane)
Orson Scott Card (author of Ender's Game)

assoc.t: Orson Welles, director and star of Citizen Kane

e.etymology: Used by Mexican and Mexican American families and linked to the Itza, the Maya people of Chichen Itza. Baby-name sources gloss it as 'gift of God', but the Mayan derivation is not well documented.
From the surname of the reformer Martin Luther, a form of the Germanic name Liuthar: liut, 'people', plus heri, 'army'. Protestants began giving it as a first name in his honor.

assoc.t: Martin Luther, leader of the Protestant Reformation
Luther, hit song by Kendrick Lamar and SZA
Lex Luthor, Superman's archenemy (spelled Luthor)
Luther, BBC crime drama starring Idris Elba

e.etymology: From the English word for a mountaintop, from Old French somete, a diminutive of som, 'top', from Latin summus, 'highest'. As a first name it is very recent.

assoc.t: summit, a mountaintop or a meeting of leaders

e.etymology: A Spanish-language name of uncertain origin, usually treated as a form of Myra, a name coined by the 17th-century English poet Fulke Greville, or of Maira.
From Hebrew Yishmael, 'God hears'. In Genesis Ishmael is Abraham's first son, by Hagar, and is traditionally counted as an ancestor of the Arabs. Ismail is the Arabic form.

assoc.t: narrator of Moby-Dick: Call me Ishmael

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Joseph in the spelling used in Egypt, the Levant and French-speaking North Africa. It goes back to Hebrew Yosef, 'he will add'; Yusuf is a prophet in the Quran.

e.meaning: dew of God (Hebrew) or blooming (Greek Thalia)
e.etymology: A spelling of Talia, especially popular in Australia. Talia is a modern Hebrew name read as 'dew of God', a form of the Greek Thalia, 'to flourish', and a short form of Natalia.
From Hebrew noam, 'pleasantness, delight', from the same root as Naomi. It is one of the most popular names in Israel, for boys and girls alike.

assoc.t: Noam Chomsky, linguist and political writer

e.etymology: From Arabic Ammar, from the root amara, 'to live long, to build, to thrive'. Ammar ibn Yasir was an early companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
